premises.logline: The Inspector measures, tags and condemns a charger cable that falls exactly one centimetre short, while a neat cable tie she wrapped round its middle sits in plain sight the whole time.
premises.audience_emotion: Fond recognition with a half-second of dread: the viewer spots the tie before she does and waits for her to find it.
premises.character_desire: To prove the cable is defective so the fault can be filed somewhere other than her.
premises.obstacle: The cable cannot reach the socket from the side table, and her procedure (tape measure, orange evidence tag) keeps confirming the gap without explaining it.
premises.escalation: Static eye-level frame. Beat 1: phone held at the cable end, short by a visible sliver. Beat 2: she lays the cable along the table and measures it. Beat 3: she tags it with safety-orange tape and tries again from a crouch. Each failed attempt tugs the cable a little taut, so the tie bunching the middle stays centre frame.
premises.surprise: She takes the cable end and slowly runs her fingers along it. Her hand stops at the tie, with the spare tie on her lanyard clearly matching it. A beat of warm disappointment. She cuts it, the cable reaches, the phone plugs in with a satisfied click.
premises.payoff: She is the culprit: her own habit of tidy-wrapping every cable ate the missing centimetre. After the fix she looks at the loose, slightly messy cable, produces a fresh tie from a flap pocket and wraps it tight again. The cable is short again; she steps back into the opening pose. The camera noticed the tie in frame one.
premises.structure: Single locked-off take. Procedure, then a fair-play reveal that is visible from the first second, then a compulsive relapse that loops back to the opening pose and a short cable.
premises.why_send_it: A viewer sends it to the friend who 'tidies' everything into a worse state, such as the one who coils the group chat's shared charger so tightly nobody can use it, with the implied message 'this is you, and you do it with love.' The loop invites a second watch to catch the tie that was there at second 0.
premises.commercial_fit: None. No brand or product is shown; the cable and phone are generic and unbranded.

premises.logline: To spare a nearly dead phone, the Inspector refuses to move the table and holds the plug at full stretch, becoming a rigid, trembling human bridge across the one-centimetre gap.
premises.audience_emotion: Escalating tension and giggling disbelief at deadpan endurance, ending in a held breath.
premises.character_desire: To keep the investigation untouched and the evidence in place, even at personal cost.
premises.obstacle: The cable will not reach, and she will not move any element of the scene because that would contaminate it.
premises.escalation: She extends her arm fully and plugs in. A tiny tremor starts. Her lamp swings on its strap. Her lanyard clipboard slowly hooks the side-table lamp's cord and drags the lamp toward the table edge, millimetre by millimetre, while her face stays composed.
premises.surprise: The lamp tips over the edge and she catches it with her free foot without breaking her rigid pose.
premises.payoff: The Inspector caused the second fault by hooking her own lanyard on the lamp cord. She returns the lamp to the table and stands in the same stretched pose, but the clipboard is already hooking the cord again. Loop.
premises.structure: Endurance gag. A single sustained physical pose that builds to a near-disaster and a tiny recovery, with a loop by relapse.
premises.why_send_it: A viewer sends it to the friend who will physically suffer rather than do the obvious, tiny thing, such as the one who stands for an hour holding a phone at an angle instead of moving the table.
premises.rejected_because: The pose is hard for generation models to hold without limb drift, and the cause of the lamp's movement is harder to read at a glance than the other premises.

premises.logline: Shot top-down like a micro-scale investigation, the Inspector's gloved hands measure the short cable while the phone creeps one centimetre further away every time she leans in.
premises.audience_emotion: Pleasure in a rhythmic, escalating pattern, plus the small thrill of seeing what she cannot.
premises.character_desire: To get an accurate, uncontested measurement of the shortfall.
premises.obstacle: The shortfall keeps changing, because the thing she is measuring keeps moving.
premises.escalation: Three repeating beats: she places the tape, leans in with the clipboard and lamp strap, and the table jolts; the phone slides one centimetre. She re-squares everything, repeats, and the phone slides further each round.
premises.surprise: On the third round the phone slides off the cable entirely, then the cable slowly slides after it, and her lanyard is revealed as the thing dragging both.
premises.payoff: Her own measuring technique creates and widens the gap. She nods in satisfaction at the 'confirmed' gap, which is now ten centimetres. Final frame returns the phone to its starting position, ready for beat one again.
premises.structure: Rhythmic triple-beat Sisyphean cycle, shot as top-down insert detail with only hands and sleeves visible.
premises.why_send_it: A viewer sends it to the friend whose 'just checking' always makes the situation worse, such as the one who re-checks a shared plan until it falls apart.
premises.rejected_because: Hands-only framing loses the Inspector's face and warm-disappointment expression, which are the core identity anchors.

premises.logline: A silent stealth swap: the Inspector tiptoes to steal a longer cable from a sleeping housemate's phone and leaves her own short one behind, until a blanket-wrapped hand quietly passes the short cable back.
premises.audience_emotion: Sneaky glee and warmth between two people who never speak.
premises.character_desire: To fix her charging problem without waking the housemate.
premises.obstacle: The housemate's sleeping phone charges on the long cable; every foley sound threatens to wake them.
premises.escalation: Exaggerated foley for each tiptoe, the clipboard clack she muffles with a sleeve, a hand sliding the plug out in slow motion, the housemate's foot twitching in the sofa corner of frame.
premises.surprise: The swap works, and the housemate's blanketed hand reaches out, takes the cable from her without opening an eye and puts the short one back in her palm.
premises.payoff: The housemate's phone now sits one centimetre short, and she is the next offender: she holds the short cable again, standing in the original pose.
premises.structure: Two-hander relay. Her heist is answered by a passed fault, ending in a handoff that loops her back to the start.
premises.why_send_it: A viewer sends it to the housemate or partner who 'borrows' the good charger and returns a worse one.
premises.rejected_because: It needs a second performer in a sleeping pose and depends on a subtle off-camera handoff that is harder to keep legible in 12 seconds.

premises.logline: Defeated by the short cable, the Inspector opens the side-table drawer for a spare and reveals dozens of identical cables, each a centimetre short and each carrying her own orange evidence tag.
premises.audience_emotion: Delighted 'oh no, that is my drawer' recognition.
premises.character_desire: To find one cable that finally works and close the case.
premises.obstacle: Every cable she tries from the drawer fails in the same way.
premises.escalation: She pulls cable after cable, tags each with a flick of orange tape and lays it on the table in a perfectly straight row, tapping the clipboard once before the last attempt.
premises.surprise: The camera reveals the drawer is packed with identical tagged cables, so she has been repeating this investigation for years.
premises.payoff: She is the culprit: she keeps buying the same wrong length. She tags the newest cable, slides it into the drawer next to the others, closes it with an exaggerated click and returns to the opening pose. Loop.
premises.structure: Cold-open problem, then a pattern reveal in the drawer and a ritual filing that loops.
premises.why_send_it: A viewer sends it to the friend with the drawer of useless chargers, with the message 'we need to talk about the drawer.'
premises.commercial_fit: None. Cables are unbranded and tags carry no readable text.
premises.rejected_because: Strong and relatable, but the reveal is a static pile-up, so the camera noticing before her is weaker than in P1.

premises.ranking_rationale: P1 best satisfies the bible rule: the cause is visible in frame one, the camera notices before she does, and her relapse makes the loop the punchline. P5 is the most shareable, with a clean reveal and a strong send target, but its payoff lands later and is less rewatchable. P3, P4 and P2 are distinct in visual language, relationship and performance mode but each carries a production or legibility risk for a 12-second single-clip silent gag.

A neat white cable tie is cinched round the middle of the cable, dead centre of frame.

hook_variants.rationale: The orange tag ritual is instantly on-brand and the tie is in frame, but the gap to the socket is less obvious in frame one than in H1.

hook_variants.first_frame: Static frame of the closed side-table drawer with the Inspector standing before it, clipboard held across her chest, a single cable lying short of the socket on the tabletop and an orange tag fluttering on it.
hook_variants.first_line_or_action: She slides the drawer open a few centimetres, and orange tags spill into view along its edge.
hook_variants.rationale: It builds a good withheld-reveal, but the first frame carries little by itself and the problem is not clear until a second or two in.

selected.rationale: H1 puts both the one-centimetre gap and the cable tie in frame one, so the muted viewer is already ahead of the Inspector, which is the bible rule in its purest form and sets up the relapse loop. The trade-off against the runner-up (P5/H5) is that the drawer hook is the more instantly sendable to a specific friend, but its payoff lands later and its camera-notices-first beat is weaker, so P1/H1 is the stronger fit for a 12-second silent loop.

script.title: One Centimetre Short
script.synopsis: In a single locked-off take, the Inspector measures, tags and condemns a phone charger cable that stops one centimetre short of the wall socket, while a neat white cable tie she wrapped herself sits in plain view mid-cable. She finally runs her fingers along the cable, finds the tie, matches it to the spare on her lanyard, cuts it, and the phone plugs in. Then she compulsively wraps a fresh tie round the loose cable, and the cable is short again as she resumes the opening pose.

beats.beat: Frame one: the Inspector holds the plug a visible sliver from the socket with the white cable tie cinched dead centre on the cable; she pushes, the cable goes taut and the tie quivers.
She lays the cable along the table, measures it with a tape, and reads the number with grave composure; the tie sits centre frame throughout.
She wraps a strip of safety-orange tape round the cable end as an evidence tag, retries from a crouch, and each failed pull tugs the cable and shakes the tie.
She runs two fingers along the cable, stops at the tie, glances at the matching spare on her lanyard, and her face settles into warm disappointment.
She cuts the tie, the cable reaches, the plug seats with a satisfied click; then she produces a fresh tie from a flap pocket and cinches it tight again.
She steps back into the opening pose holding the plug one centimetre short of the socket, tie dead centre. Loop.

script.cta: Send it to the friend who ties everything up too tight.

evidence.claim: The silent gag is legible with no words: the problem and the culprit prop are both visible in frame one.
The relapse (re-tying the cable) satisfies the bible rule that the Inspector is the culprit and the camera notices first.
evidence.source: bible inspector-v1 rule and selected premise P1

evidence.claim: A single 12 s locked-off clip with no internal cuts should be generatable in one pass, but holding the tie's position and the exact start and end pose is a risk.

evidence.originality: The self-inflicted cause being a tidy-wrapping habit, with the culprit hidden in plain sight and a compulsive re-tie relapse, is a specific, fresh twist on the familiar 'too short cable' joke.
evidence.hook: Frame one shows both the one-centimetre gap and the cinched tie, so a muted viewer is ahead of the character from second 0, though the tie is a small prop that may read weakly on a phone screen.
evidence.coherence: Cause, reveal, fix and relapse chain cleanly into the loop and the tie stays centre frame throughout, with only minor friction in S4 where she plugs in, re-ties and then must unplug to restore the gap.
evidence.identity: Anchors (glasses, straight brows, aubergine jacket, chest lamp, lanyard) recur in every scene and the neutral-to-warm-disappointment microexpression is the actual turn of the gag.
evidence.audiovisual: Every scene specifies lens, rig, lighting, ambience and named foley with no dialogue, and the sound design (tie rattle, tape tear, click) carries the gag well, though S4 adds a 'charging chime' that sits slightly outside the foley-only brief.
evidence.feasibility: Twelve seconds in one uncut clip packs tape-measuring, taping, crouching, finger-tracing, cutting, plugging, re-tying and returning to the exact opening pose, which is very dense for a generator and risks hand, cable and tie-legibility drift.
evidence.grounding: It respects single location, zero dialogue, no cuts inside clips, unbranded props and a loop ending, and the physical logic of a tie bunching cable to cost a centimetre is plausible enough.
evidence.commercial_fit: With no commercial brief it correctly stays brand-free, has a clear send-to-a-friend share motive and a disclosure line, and the caption 'Case closed. (Again.)' suits Reels.

qa_review.summary: A tidy, well-constructed loop gag whose fair-play reveal, character-driven payoff and complete audiovisual direction make it genuinely shareable. The main risk is execution: too many fine-motor beats and a small key prop in 12 uncut seconds.
qa_review.top_fix: Cut or merge beats to reduce fine-motor load in the single clip (for example drop the tape measure or the orange tag) and make the white tie larger or higher-contrast so it reads at phone size.
